title: Why do news anchors all sound the same? | NEWS WORDS

entries.note: The press and news media, also called the fourth power; the other estates are clergy, nobility and commoners, tentatively traced to [[see?:Edmund Burke]] in 1771.
The OED tentatively traces [[see:Fourth Estate]] to him, possibly in a 1771 parliamentary debate on press reporting of the House of Commons.
The journalistic practice of finding two reputable sources, which many internet sources fail to do.
A London street once full of print houses and newspaper offices, the hub of British print journalism within Rob's lifetime.
Suffix attached to any scandal through [[see:rebracketing]] of [[from:Watergate]], though gate there just means street; even used alone to mean a scandal.
The scandal whose name gave the scandal suffix [[gave:-gate]], though gate in it just means street.
Taking part of a word and attaching it to other words, as with [[see:-gate]].
Journalistic term, like [[see:off the record]], that has entered everyday use.
Journalistic term, like [[see:on the record]], that people use regularly in everyday life.
Information that can be used but whose source cannot be cited; less common in everyday speech than [[see:off the record]].
British equivalent of [[see:on background]]: you may use what you're told but not say who told you; Chatham House is a London venue; adopted by corporate America.
Named for its large paper format; broadsheets were generally the more reputable papers of record, though most have switched to the smaller [[see:Berliner]].
Originally a smaller newspaper size, now implying sensationalism; named after a trademarked medicine tablet, from [[from:tablet]] plus -oid or a blend with [[from?:alkaloid]].
The much smaller newspaper format that most former [[see:broadsheet]]s have switched to.
The top half of a [[see:broadsheet]] front page, visible when the paper is folded on a stand; now also used in web design.
The unusual word choices found in [[see:tabloid]] newspapers, especially on front pages, mostly driven by the need to save space.
[[see:tabloidese]] for child on British front pages, now dying out somewhat.
[[see:tabloidese]] used instead of referring to having sex.
[[see:tabloidese]] for a prisoner, as in a lag on the run.
[[see:tabloidese]] for experts, puzzlingly since it isn't any shorter.
[[see:tabloidese]] used in place of investigation.
[[see:tabloidese]] for an argument, now oddly common in broadcast news though it exists only to save column inches.
[[see:tabloidese]] for criticised, alongside [[see:slammed]] and [[see:rapped]].
[[see:tabloidese]] for criticised.
[[see:tabloidese]] for criticised.
[[see:tabloidese]] used instead of managers and executives.
[[see:tabloidese]] used instead of managers and executives.
The wider journalistic style of which [[see:tabloidese]] is a part, seen well beyond tabloids.
Choosing words so a headline fits its space, which explains much [[see:tabloidese]].
A headline made ambiguous by space limits, named after a 2009 Japan Today headline, Violinist linked to JAL crash blossoms.
An extreme synonym used to avoid repeating a word, named after an infamous second reference to a crocodile.
The journalist's routine second reference to a fire, though nobody actually calls a fire a blaze.
Security devices at Trump's Scottish golf course, described with the [[see:knobbly monster]] [[see:Doctor Who's croaky-voiced enemies]].
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used as the second reference to [[see:Daleks]].
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used for advent calendars.
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used for badgers.
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used for beavers.
A [[see:knobbly monster]] used for Darth Vader.
Jess's alternative for the Super Bowl to avoid repeating herself in recurring stories, like a [[see:knobbly monster]].
Arabic for storehouse, via Italian and Middle French; first a military storehouse (1580s), then a weapon's ammo holder, then periodicals after [[see:The Gentleman's Magazine]].
French word sharing its source with [[same-root:magazine]] but meaning storehouse or shop, the basic French word for a shop.
Among the first to apply [[see:magazine]] to printed miscellany, punning on storehouse; the first magazine in today's sense, with a rather masculine name.
From Italian [[from:gazzetta]], a Venetian coin that was the price of an early newspaper in Venice.
A publication costing a penny, compared with the coin-named [[see:gazette]].
From the French for daily, from Latin [[from:diurnalis]] and ultimately the Latin word for day; cognate with [[same-root:diurnal]].
Someone who writes daily, showing English did take a French day-word, from [[from:journal]].
Borrowed from Latin and cognate with [[same-root:journal]]; feels like it should relate to two but just means daily.
Its printing origin was discussed in an earlier episode.
A journalistic substitute for will that isn't how people naturally talk.
How journalists always describe something going up.
Used to link two events, implying a causal connection without stating one, as in a CBS News example.
Repeated constantly to avoid accusing uncharged people, though it is not the legal cure-all it's thought to be, especially in British law.
Used in news (it is being reported, it's understood) and crime stories to avoid attribution; generally bad form, and used in PR to avoid blame.
The unnatural intonation and pausing newsreaders adopt, which Rob found hard to train out of new readers; possibly helps keep pace with a teleprompter.
A journalistic couplet for any meeting about something bad, rarely used in everyday speech.
In news writing, reports are always damning.
In news writing, debates are always heated.
In political reporting, deals always come at the 11th hour.
A journalistic phrase rarely heard outside political reporting.
A legal anaphoric adverb, compared with condensed journalistic phrases like [[see:crisis talks]].
A legal anaphoric adverb, compared with condensed journalistic phrases like [[see:crisis talks]].
A story's opening paragraph, deliberately respelled from lead to avoid confusion with the metal [[see:lead]] and [[see:leading]] used in typesetting.
An expression using the newsroom sense of [[see:lede]].
In typesetting, the vertical space between lines of text; discussed in their typography and printing episode.
The metal, and in typesetting a piece of spacing material, which could also be called a [[see:slug]].
A cast line of hot type, perhaps for its shape; also a short label for a story, now in URLs; possibly tied to slug meaning bullet.
What Rob thinks a [[see:slug]] would be called if invented today.
Newsroom spelling of head(line): shorter for margins and avoids confusion with words like [[see:headshot]] or adding head to the text.
Someone's picture; the spelling [[see:hed]] avoids confusion with it.
A mini headline dividing a story into sections, also written with the [[see:hed]] spelling.
The text below a headline explaining more, often reused as social media copy; spelled dek or deck, a transatlantic difference.
The nutshell paragraph explaining a story's essential point; nut is the core essence, and [[see:graf]] is short for paragraph.
Shortening of [[from:paragraph]], spelled so for speed and to avoid confusion with a graph.
Short for to come, marking something to fill in later, as in pre-written obituaries; spelled TK because that combination is rare in English.
Text for publication, reproduced in many copies; every sense comes from Latin [[from:copia]], abundance, relating it to [[same-root:cornucopia]] and [[same-root:copious]].
Related to [[same-root:copy]] through Latin copia, abundance.
Related to [[same-root:copy]] through Latin copia.
Checks that [[see:copy]] is clean and follows house style, traditionally sitting at the copy desk.
Write marketing [[see:copy]], so called because the words are reused across a brand's many media.
[[see:Ian Betteridge]]'s 2009 maxim that any headline ending in a question mark can be answered no, prompted by a TechCrunch headline about Last.fm.
British journalist behind [[see:Betteridge's law]], stated in a throwaway 2009 blog post; he told Rob he hoped it improved headline writing.
Means opposite the editorial, not opinion; usually an opinion piece by a guest contributor, unlike a [[see:column]].
For Jess, distinct from an [[see:op-ed]]: usually written by a recurring contributor.
Common articles that often start with a question headline, which is fine when the question is actually answered, unlike cases covered by [[see:Betteridge's law]].
The same energy as question-mark headlines: making heavy, potentially actionable implications in [[see:bad faith]].
The term for [[see:just asking questions]]-style implication.
Its 1916 election headline Hughes elected in close contest? was technically right when [[see:Woodrow Wilson]] won, though it pictured President-elect [[see:Charles Evans Hughes]].
Reported by other papers as election winner; the [[see:New York World]] hedged with a question mark.
Actually won the election the [[see:New York World]] hedged on.
Sending the paper off for printing; London papers bound for Scotland had to be put to bed early.

Sensationalist news, coined in the 1890s circulation wars of [[see:Joseph Pulitzer]] and [[see:William Randolph Hearst]], named after [[from:The Yellow Kid]]; perhaps reinforced by yellow meaning cowardice.
Owner of the New York World, whose papers ran [[see:The Yellow Kid]] in the rivalry behind [[see:yellow journalism]].
Owner of the New York Journal, Pulitzer's rival in the circulation wars behind [[see:yellow journalism]].
An early entertainment comic strip in Pulitzer's papers that became emblematic of the rivalry, giving [[gave:yellow journalism]].
In that era meant a street mutt, another negative association of yellow; gave [[gave:yellow dog Democrat]].
A 19th-century Southern Democrat who would vote for a [[from:yellow dog]] before a Republican.
A term similar in idea to [[see:yellow journalism]], recalling the street dog.
Wild, subjective first-person reporting made famous by [[see:Hunter S. Thompson]]; [[see:Bill Cardoso]] used [[from:gonzo]] to describe his style.
Made [[see:gonzo journalism]] famous with [[see:The Kentucky Derby Is Decadent and Depraved]].

entries.term: The Kentucky Derby Is Decadent and Depraved
entries.note: [[see:Hunter S. Thompson]]'s piece about the spectators rather than the race, the defining example of [[see:gonzo journalism]].
Described [[see:Hunter S. Thompson]]'s style as [[see:gonzo]].
Probably Italian slang for loud or obnoxious, earlier jazz slang for raucous music; the Italian may come from a word for goose.
The Muppet debuted in 1970 but was only named after [[from?:gonzo journalism]] got its name, probably intentionally.
A [[see:knobbly monster]] for Kermit the Frog, one of [[see:Gonzo]]'s friends.
Jess's improvised [[see:knobbly monster]] for Kermit the Frog.
Coined pejoratively by [[see:Theodore Roosevelt]] in 1906, alluding to [[from:The Pilgrim's Progress]]; adopted proudly by early 20th-century investigative journalists exposing corruption.
Coined [[see:muckraking]] pejoratively in 1906 with his man with the muck rake.
Its man with the muck rake can look only downward and sees only filth, the image behind [[see:muckraking]].
A clichéd ending for news reports; Rob used it in his first report and a colleague told him never to write it again.
